doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

title: Industry molds and the loss of artist development
summary: Today's labels push artists into a few molds and skip artist development, but individual voices last.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: it’s literally like three artists you’ve got to fit in that mold. If you’re a black singer and you are a male you’ve got to fit somewhere in the Chris Brown mold. You know? If you’re female you’ve got to fit in the Beyoncé mold. You know I went to high school with Beyoncé. So that’s another individual that I know — I knew her for a long time. You know. But those are certain molds that people say okay, now we need you to be like that because that makes money, versus people taking the time. You know they used to even have a thing called Artist Development in record labels. They would sign somebody and put you through the wringer to help you figure out how to do shows and be on stage, talk to the press, all these things. Now they just sign you and throw you out there. Because they just want to make the quick dollar. Especially now, because record labels are folding and all that. So that don’t have no time for no artist development, they don’t care. You know? But you know the artists that have the individual voice are the artists that last. And those are the artists that people remember. You know, that’s just a real thing.
I think relative to the students, it’s really important for them to think about the same things for themselves.
